canonical_question: How does the 'good refractory property' of the HEA NW at 1000 K quantitatively compare to the decay observed in Silver (Ag) nanowires at the same temperature?

question_variants.question: How does the 'good refractory property' of the HEA NW at 1000 K quantitatively compare to the decay observed in Silver (Ag) nanowires at the same temperature?
question_variants.resolution_summary: The HEA nanowire exhibits 'good refractory property' at 1000 K by maintaining ductility and avoiding rapid failure, whereas Silver (Ag) nanowires at the same temperature show a rapid decay in flow stress and ductility, leading to failure. The HEA behavior is attributed to synergistic deformation mechanisms, while Ag fails by necking at partial dislocation junctions.

answers.answer: The HEA nanowire maintains better mechanical properties at 1000 K due to synergistic interactions of deformation twinning, FCC-HCP phase transformation, and cross-section reorientation. In contrast, Silver (Ag) nanowires at 1000 K suffer from rapid decay in flow stress and ductility, fulfilling failure conditions quickly.
answers.measurement_outcome: HEA shows 'synergistic result' maintaining properties; Ag shows decay of flow stress and ductility to failure.
answers.mechanism: HEA: Synergistic twinning, phase transformation, reorientation. Ag: Decay due to lack of stabilizing mechanisms at high T.
answers.boundary_limitation: Qualitative comparison provided; no quantitative ratio of decay rates given for Ag.
evidence_spans: In high entropy alloy (HEA) CoNiCrFeMn nanowires, the motion of the partial dislocation is hindered by the friction due to difference in the lattice parameter of the constituent atoms which is responsible for the hardening and lowering the ductility.
In this study, we have examined the temperature-dependent superplasticity of single component Ag and multicomponent CoNiCrFeMn HEA nanowires using molecular dynamics simulations.
The results demonstrate that Ag nanowires exhibit apparent temperature-dependent superplasticity at cryogenic temperature due to (110) to (100) cross-section reorientation behavior.
